title: Work site insecticide, herbicide or fungicide clean-up and clearance processes

lessons.title: Finishing the treatment and controlling re-entry
lessons.html:
Finishing the treatment and controlling re-entry

A pest control job is not finished when the sprayer is switched off. As a pest management officer you are responsible for the site until it has been cleaned up and formally handed back. Many poisoning incidents happen after the application, when workers, children or animals walk into a treated grain store, packshed or field too early.

Immediately after application

  • Stop application and close the product containers. Put them back in the locked vehicle chemical box, not on the ground.
  • Check that no product has drifted outside the target area, for example onto a neighbour's vegetables, a borehole, a dam or the workers' houses.
  • Leave warning signs at all entrances to the treated area. The sign should say what was applied, the date and time, and when people may enter again.
  • Keep doors of treated buildings closed if the label asks for it, then ventilate as the label instructs before people return.

Re-entry periods

Every registered agricultural remedy (Act 36 of 1947) has a label. The label states the re-entry interval and, for crops, the withholding period before harvest or grazing. Never guess these values and never shorten them because the client is in a hurry. If the label is unclear, phone the product supplier or registration holder before you give clearance.

Tell the person in charge of the site, in writing, when it is safe to re-enter. On a farm this is usually the farm manager or foreman, who must tell the workers in their own language. Ask them to keep livestock out of treated veld or camps for the period on the label.

Check the site before you leave

Walk through the treated area. Look for puddles of mix, wet spots on surfaces where food is handled, dead pests that pets or poultry could eat, and spilt granules or bait. Remove or cover these. Bait stations must be secured and recorded on a site plan so that they can be found and checked later.

lessons.title: Cleaning equipment and handling spills
lessons.html:
Cleaning equipment and handling spills

Equipment left with chemical inside it damages pumps, seals and nozzles, and the next job can be contaminated. A knapsack that sprayed a herbicide and is then used for insecticide in a vegetable tunnel can kill the crop. Clean equipment at the end of every job.

Where to clean

  • Use a set wash-down area away from boreholes, rivers, dams, drains and food stores. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 makes it an offence to pollute water resources.
  • Choose a place where rinse water can be caught or sprayed back onto the treated target area, as the label allows.
  • Never wash sprayers in a stream, a cattle trough or the farm dam.

Cleaning steps

  1. Wear the same PPE you used for mixing: gloves, eye protection, overall and boots, plus a respirator if the label requires it.
  2. Empty any leftover mix onto the treated area at the label rate. Do not tip it out in one spot.
  3. Rinse the tank, hose, lance and nozzles with clean water. Spray the rinse water onto the treated area.
  4. Remove nozzles and filters, clean them with a soft brush and water. Never blow through a nozzle with your mouth.
  5. Use a tank cleaner where the label says so, especially after hormone-type herbicides.
  6. Rinse again, check for leaks and store the equipment dry and locked away.

Empty containers

Triple rinse empty containers: fill a quarter with water, close, shake, and pour the rinse into the spray tank. Repeat three times. Puncture the container so it cannot be reused for water or food, and keep it in a locked area until it goes to an approved collection or recycling point.

Spills

If product spills: keep people and animals away, stop the source, contain the spill with sand, soil or absorbent, scoop it into a marked container and report it. Never hose a spill into a drain. If anyone is exposed, follow the first aid instructions on the label and get medical help, taking the label with you.

lessons.title: Waste, records and handing over the site
lessons.html:
Waste, records and handing over the site

The last part of the job is to remove all waste, record what was done and hand the site back to the client in a safe condition. This protects the people on the site and protects you and your company if there is a complaint later.

Waste

  • Contaminated absorbent, used filters, damaged PPE and rinsed containers are hazardous waste. Keep them in a marked, closed container in your vehicle.
  • Take waste to an approved hazardous waste site or a container collection scheme. Never burn containers or bury them on the farm.
  • Keep proof of disposal with the job file.

Personal clean-up

Wash gloves before taking them off. Remove PPE, wash hands and face with soap before eating, drinking or smoking. Wash overalls separately from family clothes. If you feel headache, nausea, dizziness or blurred vision after a job, stop work and get medical help.

The job record

RecordExample
Site and area treatedSilo complex, bins 3 and 4
Target pestGrain weevil
Product, registration number, batchAs on the label
Rate and total volume usedFrom your calibration
Weather at applicationWind, temperature
Re-entry and withholding periodFrom the label
Operator and signatureName, registration

Clearance and hand-over

Before clearance, check that the re-entry period has passed, ventilation is complete, signs are still in place until clearance, and no residues or waste remain. Walk the site with the client's representative. Explain what was used, any precautions still needed and when follow-up visits are planned. Both parties sign the clearance or service certificate. Only then may the signs be removed and normal work start again.

Key points

  • The site stays your responsibility until it is formally cleared and handed back.
  • Re-entry and withholding periods come from the product label; never shorten them.
  • Clean equipment and rinse containers away from water sources and spray rinse onto the target area.
  • Treat contaminated materials as hazardous waste and keep proof of disposal.
  • Record every job fully and get a signed clearance from the client.
